items.answer: Duplicate images could appear in both the training and the test set, so the model has already seen the test images and the scores look too high. Imputing the missing labels from the radiologist notes meant we did not have to throw those images away.
Because duplicates leak between train and test, the results become over-optimistic, so we removed them. We also imputed labels using the radiologist notes to keep more images.

If the same scan is in both the learning part and the evaluation part, the model is graded on something it memorised, which makes the numbers look better than they really are. For unlabeled scans we copied the label from the doctor's written notes rather than deleting them.
We removed duplicates because they can leak between the training and test sets.
Missing labels were imputed so we did not lose data.
leak inflate imputation radiologist duplicates train test
Because it is good practice to clean data before training.
To make the model train faster.

Random Forest can capture non-linear interactions between features, so we did not need manual feature engineering. Logistic Regression is faster and easier to interpret, but it scored clearly lower on validation.

The data has complex relationships that a linear model misses; the forest handles interactions automatically without handcrafting features, and since logistic regression was simpler but worse on the validation set, the forest was the better baseline.

The signals in the images interact with each other in curved, not straight-line ways, and a forest learns that by itself so nobody had to design extra inputs by hand. The straight-line model was quicker to run and easier to explain but its results on held-out data were worse.
Random Forest works better with non-linear data.
Logistic Regression is simpler and faster but Random Forest scored higher on validation.
non-linear interaction feature engineering interpret faster validation scored lower
Because Random Forest is a popular algorithm.
Because it has more trees so it must be better.

Only about 12% of the images show a finding, so the classes are imbalanced. A model that always predicts no finding would get about 88% accuracy while detecting nothing, which makes accuracy misleading. F1 uses precision and recall of the positive class, so it only goes up when findings are actually found.

Because of the class imbalance, accuracy is misleading: predicting the majority class gives 88%. F1 balances precision and recall on the minority class, so it reflects how well the rare cases are caught.

Most scans are healthy, so a lazy model that says healthy every time looks great on accuracy yet misses every sick patient. The team wanted a number that punishes missed sick patients and false alarms, which is what the F1 score does.
Accuracy is misleading when classes are imbalanced.
F1 combines precision and recall.
imbalance 12% 88 misleading precision recall minority
Because F1 is a better metric in general.
The professor told us to use F1.

Stratification keeps the same proportion of positive images in train, validation and test. With a purely random split, a small test set could get very few positives by chance, which would make the F1 estimate unstable.

A random split could leave the small test set with no positive images, so F1 would be noisy and unreliable; stratifying keeps the class distribution the same in every subset and makes results comparable.

Only a small fraction of scans are sick, and with only a few thousand images the luck of the draw could put almost all of them in one part. Splitting separately inside each class means every part gets its fair share, so the final score is dependable.
A stratified split keeps the same share of positive images in each subset.
A random split can give a test set with few positives.
stratified same proportion random split few positive unstable
Because stratified splits are standard.
To make the dataset bigger.

All the images come from one hospital and one scanner type, so we cannot claim the model generalises to other hospitals or scanners. External validation on another hospital's data is needed before anyone relies on it.
The data comes from a single hospital, so there may be a domain shift to other scanners and populations; the report says the model was not tested elsewhere and needs external validation.

Everything we trained and tested on was collected at the same site with the same machine, so we simply don't know if it works on scans from elsewhere; the honest thing is to say so and to check it on fresh data from a different clinic before using it.
The model was only tested on one hospital's images.
We need external validation on other data.
one hospital generalise scanner population external validation
Because we did not have time to test it.
Because the model is not good enough.
